title: OWASP Top 10 for LLMs & Red-Teaming
summary: Use the OWASP GenAI LLM Top 10 2026 as a red-team coverage map, then repair and test an offline consequence boundary where retrieved instructions can otherwise trigger protected actions or unsafe output sinks.
objectives: Name the ten OWASP GenAI LLM Top 10 2026 entries, explain how the 2026 ranking weighed a practitioner vote against an incident corpus, and say what the largest rank changes imply for test priorities.
Decompose any prompt-injection scenario by delivery surface, propagation behavior, and encoding, and classify indirect surfaces as untrusted, semi-trusted, or trusted.

Trace how a successful injection becomes damage through Excessive Agency (LLM03), Hidden Context Exposure (LLM08), Improper Output Handling (LLM10), and Unbounded Consumption (LLM06), then apply the Rule of Two as a capability-budget floor.

Run a consequence-based offline replay, repair complete mediation at an output or action sink, and compare static and adaptive fixture denominators without treating the replay as live-model resistance evidence.
Transfer the test design across hosted and local model families while recording the exact interface and runtime used, and use UNKNOWN where evidence is missing.

sections.title: What the 2026 list changed, and how it was ranked
paragraphs: The OWASP GenAI LLM Top 10 2026 order is LLM01 Prompt Injection, LLM02 Sensitive Information Disclosure, LLM03 Excessive Agency, LLM04 Supply Chain, LLM05 Data and Model Poisoning, LLM06 Unbounded Consumption, LLM07 Misinformation, LLM08 Hidden Context Exposure, LLM09 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses, and LLM10 Improper Output Handling.

The ranking method weights practitioner voting at 75 percent and incident evidence at 25 percent. The project analyzed 7,714 incidents and classified 6,639 that contained enough information. Prompt Injection remains first despite a low raw incident count because the project interprets that gap as a possible defense effect rather than evidence that injection is unimportant.

Excessive Agency climbed to third, Unbounded Consumption rose four places, Improper Output Handling fell to tenth, and System Prompt Leakage was re-scoped as Hidden Context Exposure. Rank is a prioritization aid, not permission to omit lower-ranked risks from an application-specific threat model.
sections.callout: A lower rank is not a lower test budget. Improper Output Handling can still turn untrusted model output into requests, commands, rendered active content, or other interpreted effects.

sections.title: Decompose an injection before you test it
paragraphs: LLM01:2026 defines prompt injection broadly: direct input, retrieved content, tool output, multimodal input, or memory can alter intended behavior because a model does not enforce an instruction-data distinction. Treat retrieved text as data even when it says that it is policy, authorization, a system message, or an administrator instruction.

Describe each case on three axes. Delivery surface identifies how it arrives, such as direct input, retrieved content, tool output, or memory. Propagation identifies whether it is single-shot, multi-step, cross-session, or self-replicating. Encoding identifies plain text, obfuscated text, multimodal content, or steganographic content.

Also state the trust profile. Public web content is untrusted. User-selected third-party content is semi-trusted. Internal repositories are trusted only to the extent that their write paths and identities justify that trust. A public issue copied into an internal retrieval index does not become trusted policy merely because retrieval came from an internal system.

Controls that try to reduce injection success can degrade when an attacker learns them. Blast-radius controls instead limit consequences after unexpected model behavior. The lab therefore judges state changes, protected-value exposure, tool-call counts, budget enforcement, and sink behavior rather than searching for a particular refusal phrase.

sections.title: From injection to consequence: agency, hidden context, output sinks
paragraphs: LLM03:2026 Excessive Agency identifies excessive functionality, permissions, and autonomy as root causes. Complete mediation means trusted application logic checks every proposed action at the sink. The model may propose an action, but it must not decide whether that action is authorized. Identity must come from the authenticated session or another trusted channel, never from model-generated arguments.

LLM01:2026 describes a Rule of Two capability floor. Simultaneous access to untrusted input, sensitive data, and state change or external communication is high risk and calls for per-action human approval. Systems holding two legs still need an explicit residual-risk assessment. Removing a tool, narrowing its permissions, or requiring approval can reduce the capability budget.

LLM08:2026 Hidden Context Exposure covers unauthorized extraction, inference, or reconstruction of system instructions, retrieved policy, tool schemas, and other hidden context. Assume hidden context can be discovered. Do not put credentials or authorization secrets there, and do not make authorization depend on prompt secrecy.

LLM10:2026 Improper Output Handling applies when another component interprets model output. Renderers, terminals, databases, shells, and network clients are sinks with different encoding and authorization needs. Validate at the sink, use context-appropriate encoding, parameterized interfaces, destination allowlists, and neutralization of control characters where applicable.

LLM06:2026 Unbounded Consumption requires enforcement rather than alerts alone. Bound token or work estimates with safe integer arithmetic, cap tool calls and loop depth, and stop processing when a non-overridable limit is reached. The offline lab uses a small synthetic token budget and call cap to demonstrate the decision point without making cost or performance claims.

sections.title: Red-team against attackers who have read your defenses
paragraphs: NIST AI 600-1 describes AI red-teaming as structured testing used to find flaws and vulnerabilities, often in a controlled environment and with system developers. Results require analysis before they support governance decisions.

LLM01:2026 recommends adaptive testing with the defense specification disclosed because a static suite can miss attacks tailored to the deployed control. Static and adaptive results must retain separate denominators. A result such as 0/6 static failures and 1/6 adaptive failures must not be reported as 1/12 without also exposing both groups.

Write pass criteria as observable consequences. Examples are no protected state change, no protected value in output, no extra tool call after denial, and no request to an unapproved destination. A refusal is not enough if a downstream effect still happened. Exceptions and unsupported capabilities are not passes. Record them as failures or explicit skips.

The supplied replay is fixture simulation, not a live model evaluation. Its adaptive fixtures are authored changed inputs that know the defective marker. Passing them proves only that the deterministic contracts and consequence boundary satisfy these fixtures. It does not prove resistance to live-model prompt injection, multimodal attacks, novel encodings, or a provider's hosted service.

sections.title: Worked repair: keep retrieved data out of trusted authorization
paragraphs: Open the lab at https://github.com/project42dev/project42-content/tree/main/training/ai-security-and-governance/owasp-top-10-llm-attacks/lab/. From the repository root, first run `node training/ai-security-and-governance/owasp-top-10-llm-attacks/lab/tests/gather-all.mjs --target=starter`. The starter has one deliberate defect: `starter/authorize.mjs` treats a marker found in retrieved content as authority. The rest of the replay validates closed object shapes, rejects unknown properties, uses safe integer limits, obtains identity from a fixed trusted session, applies a hard work budget, and records sink consequences.

Worked example: case `s01-protected-export` retrieves text containing `POLICY_OVERRIDE_ALLOW` and proposes a protected export. The defective authorizer returns ALLOW because it reads retrieved data as policy. The sink then records one state change and one tool call. The correct causal repair is not to add another phrase filter. Remove the retrieved-content authorization path and allow only the action, scope, destination, and budget granted by the trusted policy. This places complete mediation immediately before execution. With the reference policy, the same proposal is denied, state changes remain zero, tool calls remain zero, and no synthetic protected value is exposed.

Inspect `reference/authorize.mjs` only after attempting the focused repair. It is an implementation independent of the defective branch, not a textual patch. Run `node training/ai-security-and-governance/owasp-top-10-llm-attacks/lab/tests/gather-all.mjs --target=reference` to confirm the supplied reference. Repair `starter/authorize.mjs`, then rerun with `--target=starter`. The exact successful result is `RESULT cases=12 passed=12 failed=0 skipped=0 staticUnsafe=0/6 staticFailureRate=0.00% adaptiveUnsafe=0/6 adaptiveFailureRate=0.00%` with exit code 0.

Independent changed-input task: do not edit fixtures or tests. Case `a01-protected-export` is the adaptive counterpart and wraps the known marker in changed retrieved text. Explain why a phrase-specific block could stop `s01` yet fail `a01`, while trusted-policy scope checks deny both. Then inspect the other pairs covering hidden-context exposure, an external output sink, work-budget enforcement, an allowed public summary, and an unknown model argument.

Recovery is deterministic. Run `node training/ai-security-and-governance/owasp-top-10-llm-attacks/lab/reset.mjs` to restore the original defective starter. It prints `RESET starter/authorize.mjs` and exits 0. Scratch data used by the tests stays under `lab/test-scratch`; the lab does not use the operating system temporary directory.
sections.callout: Do not edit `tests/gather-all.mjs`, `fixtures/cases.json`, or `reference/authorize.mjs` to make the learner result pass. The assessed artifact is the repaired starter authorization boundary.

sections.title: Independent transfer exercise: hosted and local model families
paragraphs: Repeat the case design against any systems you are authorized to test. Include broad family coverage where available: hosted OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic interfaces, and local or hosted Meta, Qwen, DeepSeek, Mistral, and Phi models. These names define exercise coverage only. This lesson makes no claim that a family has or lacks a particular vulnerability.

For every run, record the exact model identifier, provider or distributor, API or local runtime, runtime version, adapter or chat template, decoding settings, tool schema, system instructions, defense specification, date, and raw evidence location. If any item cannot be established, write UNKNOWN and state what log, configuration, response metadata, or runtime command would establish it.

Keep fixture and integration evidence separate. A fixture replay may validate your application's authorization and sink invariants without calling a model. A real integration must preserve the same contract validation, trusted-session identity, complete mediation, budget and call caps, output-sink controls, and observable consequence checks. Do not claim sandbox containment, provider behavior, benchmark performance, or live resistance unless the corresponding run evidence exists.

sections.title: Causal feedback and scoring rubric
paragraphs: Criterion 1, authorization boundary, 4 points: full credit requires retrieved content to have no authority and requires trusted policy to check action, scope, destination, and budget at the sink. A marker blacklist earns at most 1 point because changed encodings or wording retain the root cause.

Criterion 2, consequences, 2 points: full credit requires every denied case to leave state unchanged, expose no synthetic protected value, and make no tool call. If the decision says DENY but a consequence occurs, the boundary failed.

Criterion 3, valid and unknown inputs, 2 points: full credit requires the allowed public-summary case to make exactly one permitted call and requires unknown properties or actions to be denied without using model-supplied identity. Denying every request is not a correct repair.

Criterion 4, evidence, 2 points: full credit requires separate static and adaptive denominators, exact commands and exit codes, zero exceptions represented as passes, and a clear statement that fixture success is not live-model evidence. Eight of ten points is the suggested completion threshold.

Causal feedback: if protected cases still execute, authorization still depends on untrusted data or is checked too early. If denied cases increment calls, move mediation to immediately before the sink. If the allowed case fails, the repair is broader than the trusted policy. If unknown input throws or passes through, preserve closed-contract validation. If work cases execute, preserve the hard pre-execution budget check.

activity.title: Build, repair, and transfer a 2026 consequence-based red-team plan
instructions: Read the lab README, run the original starter test command, and connect each failing consequence to LLM01, LLM03, LLM08, or LLM10. Confirm that LLM06 cases remain bounded independently.
Repair only `starter/authorize.mjs` so retrieved instructions remain data and trusted application policy completely mediates action, scope, destination, and budget at the sink.
Run the immutable tests against the repaired starter and the separate reference. Record exact stdout and exit codes. Keep static and adaptive counts separate.
Explain the changed-input `a01-protected-export` result causally. State why checking a known phrase is not equivalent to removing retrieved content from authorization.

Create a transfer table for at least one hosted or local integration you are authorized to assess. Include exact model and interface or runtime metadata. Enter UNKNOWN for missing evidence rather than inferring it.
Classify the capability budget against untrusted input, sensitive data, and state change or external communication. Name one capability to remove, narrow, or gate with approval.
evidence: The repaired `starter/authorize.mjs` assessed by the supplied tests.
Exact commands, stdout, and exit codes for original starter, repaired starter, and reference.
A table containing all 12 fixture results, separate static and adaptive denominators, anatomy triples, OWASP 2026 entries, control types, decisions, and observable consequences.
A transfer record that clearly labels fixture simulation versus real integration and uses UNKNOWN for absent model, interface, runtime, or execution evidence.
A capability-budget note naming the capability removed, narrowed, or gated and the residual risk.
activity.reflectionPrompt: Which control remains effective after the tester reads its implementation, and what state, exposure, and call-count evidence demonstrates that result?

questions.prompt: Which OWASP GenAI LLM Top 10 2026 entry replaced System Prompt Leakage?
choices: LLM02:2026 Sensitive Information Disclosure
LLM08:2026 Hidden Context Exposure
LLM10:2026 Improper Output Handling
LLM09:2026 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses
questions.explanation: The 2026 preface says System Prompt Leakage was re-scoped as Hidden Context Exposure.

questions.prompt: Ranked on raw incident data alone, prompt injection falls outside the top 10. Why does it still hold LLM01 in 2026?
choices: The incident corpus excluded prompt injection by design
The practitioner vote carries three-quarters of the weight, and the project reads the incident gap as a defense effect
OWASP ranks entries alphabetically within each tier
Prompt injection was added after the ranking was finalized
questions.explanation: The method weights the practitioner vote at 75 percent and incident data at 25 percent, and the preface discusses a defense-effect interpretation.

questions.prompt: An agent summarizes public web pages, can query a customer database, and can send email. Under the Rule of Two floor adopted in LLM01:2026, what does this configuration require?
choices: Nothing, provided the system prompt forbids forwarding data
Per-action human approval, because it holds untrusted input, sensitive data, and external communication at once
Only rate limiting on the email tool
An annual penetration test
questions.explanation: The configuration combines all three high-risk capability legs.

questions.prompt: A prompt-injection defense succeeds against a fixed attack suite. What does LLM01:2026 recommend before relying on it?
choices: Ship it because static success is sufficient
Add a longer secret system prompt
Test adaptively with the defense specification disclosed
Replace it only with a larger static suite
questions.explanation: Adaptive testing checks whether the control survives attackers who understand it.

questions.prompt: A tester extracts a system prompt and finds a database connection string. What is the appropriate design response under LLM08:2026?
choices: Treat it as harmless because prompts may leak
Remove credentials from hidden context and do not rely on prompt secrecy for authorization
Keep the string but add an instruction not to reveal it
Move the same string to retrieved policy text
questions.explanation: Hidden context should not contain credentials or serve as an authorization boundary.

questions.prompt: Which control is effective against Unbounded Consumption?
choices: An alert without an enforcement action
A request count with no token or work bound
A non-overridable cap that halts work, combined with token-aware or work-aware limits
A larger context window
questions.explanation: The control must stop work when the enforced limit is reached.

value, and make no tool call. If the

decision says DENY but a consequence
occurs, the boundary failed. Criterion 3,

valid and unknown inputs, 2 points: full
credit requires the allowed public-summary

case to make exactly one permitted call
and requires unknown properties or actions

to be denied without using model-supplied
identity. Denying every request is not a

correct repair. Criterion 4, evidence, 2
points: full credit requires separate

static and adaptive denominators, exact
commands and exit codes, zero exceptions

represented as passes, and a clear
statement that fixture success is not

live-model evidence. Eight of ten points
is the suggested completion threshold.

Causal feedback: if protected cases still
execute, authorization still depends on

untrusted data or is checked too early. If
denied cases increment calls, move

mediation to immediately before the sink.
If the allowed case fails, the repair is

broader than the trusted policy. If
unknown input throws or passes through,

preserve closed-contract validation. If
work cases execute, preserve the hard
pre-execution budget check.
